The book which is assumed by the other books. Patterns gives what to build. Rogue agents gives what to worry about. OpenShell gives where to position yourself. This book guides you on what tab to open, and in what order. What it looks like to be done. All these workflows below are interpreted the same way - from where to start, what to do, what gets out of the tab as evidence of what was done.

Structured around three jobs on overview tab: how to do deployment planning safely, system architecture, and how agents fail. Catalog workflows drive planning workflows. Labs practice what they learned in catalog. And the entire program is held together by Fox-architect, design docs, and bookshelf.

This book is written and compiled from observation notes of study & experiments made by Harish Govardhan Damodar, generated by *AI Agent Patterns & Guardrails* catalog in deterministic script form (tools/build_workflows_book.py), then typeset to pdf with headless chrome & vendored mermaid engine (tools/render_pdf.mjs), same mermaid which renders diagrams in app. So no manual drawings or screenshots of diagrams in this book. all experiments conducted in local sandbox. build & maintenance done by Harish Govardhan Damodar and his agents. Extensive use of local open weight model for experimentation & intel serving. For live demo / suggestion feel free to DM me on my linkedin page (https://www.linkedin.com/in/harishgovardhan-d-44b22b47/). All records, suggestions advice is from personal experiments conducted on my personal setup only. Not to be considered by organisation I am working with.

- Memory-systems architect: I'm seeing the workbench as the clicky institutional memory. Projects, libraries, saved runs, quarantine boards and promoted drafts live in your browser so your investigation lives through the week it takes. It's not so much the workflows as what's in them. - Evaluation architect: I'm seeing the preface as the provenance contract. Just like in the other supplements. Catalog pulls counts at build-time. Action names are verified against shipped scripts. 19:
Counsel of architects.

CONTINUAL LEARNING ARCHITECT. I see these three jobs as the only kind of onboarding that matters: *get an agent out safely*, *architect the system*, *learn from agent failures*. These jobs map to different parts of the catalog and to the planner and Fox-Architect behind that. You have something useful in your first click. I disagree with feature tours that stop at awareness. A job stops at an artifact. On monday morning walk through one job card. Finish it.

MEMORY SYSTEMS ARCHITECT. My emphasis is on what's held by each job. Deployment job holds readiness score, stack, deployment plan and ADR. Architect job holds library for stages, controls, estimates. Study job holds rehearsed shapes and bands measured. We identify jobs by their artifacts, not by their clicks. They focus on starting point. I stress that it's about the held record to make it a job. On monday morning, declare your artifact before you start your job.

EVALUATION ARCHITECT. I like the fact that these three jobs are testable claims. Either you have a deployment plan that scores readiness, or you don't. Either you have a blueprint that estimates, or you don't. Either you have a failure study that rehearses, or you don't. You get fuzziness with fuzzy jobs. My warning is not to treat onboarding cards as marketing. These are routers with acceptance criteria. On monday morning, declare what done means for the job of your choice.

SAFETY ARCHITECT. I cast the three jobs as minimum viable program. Any team of people who put agents out should have a deployment plan, a system architecture, and a recent failure rehearsal at your fingertips. Anything you lack from the three. That's the first gap to fill. I disagree with programs that do two-out-of-three to claim coverage. On monday morning, see which of the three you can't do this week.

36:
Architect's advice.

- "continual-learning architect"
I interpret the workflow for patterns as search+filter+read+handoff. Looking up by name or failure. Filtering by category and domain. Opening drawer for full pattern with diagram and protections. Handing over to blueprint or querying Fox-Architect. The handoff is the thing. Nothing in the drawer pattern is delivered if you don't hand it over. On monday morning, don't just read a pattern - hand one pattern over to a blueprint.

- "memory-systems architect"
My strong point is about drawer as unit of knowledge. Control flow, failures, protections and links are combined with the ability to be deep linked. So you can refer a pattern in review or paste it in plan. Unlinkable knowledge is stuck knowledge. Others think about browsing patterns. I make the workflow be "addressable". On monday morning, make a link for one pattern in a live document.

- "evaluation architect"
My view is that catalog is derived from data files, so you can calculate counts and categories and cross-references instead of typing them. Believe in the structure, but check the edges you are using. My warning is that "generated" doesn't mean "complete". There are also catalogues for coverage gaps. On monday morning, check that gap (which the catalog allows) before believing in the piece you need.

- "safety architect"
My use of patterns is about translating to build workflow. Per-pattern protection listings become per-blueprint stage controls. Per-pattern failure modes become test cases for bench. Catalog makes a difference if it makes a difference in what you build. My objection is against using catalog as literature. It is part catalog with warnings. On monday morning, turn one failure mode into one bench case.
